opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been pretty dramatic. If you look at the price per token for a given level of capability, it's dropped by something like two orders of magnitude, maybe more, since late 2022. And I think it's not one thing. It's a stack of improvements that compound on each other.

At the bottom you have hardware. Each GPU generation gives you more compute and, importantly, more memory bandwidth, and inference, especially decoding, is very memory-bound. Going from A100 to H100 to Blackwell, plus lower precision support like FP8 and now FP4, gives you a big multiplier on its own.

Then there's the systems and kernel layer, which is where I've spent a lot of my time. Things like FlashAttention, paged attention for managing the KV cache, continuous batching, speculative decoding, better kernels for matrix multiplies at low precision. When ChatGPT came out, a lot of serving stacks were frankly pretty inefficient. You were leaving maybe 5x or 10x on the table just from not utilizing the hardware well. The open-source inference engines and the in-house stacks at the labs closed a lot of that gap.

Then there's the model side, which I think people underappreciate. We've learned to get the same quality out of much smaller models. Better data, training way past "Chinchilla-optimal" because you care about inference cost not just training cost, distillation from bigger models. A model you could run cheaply today matches what used to require a huge model. And architecture changes help too: mixture-of-experts so you only activate a fraction of the parameters per token, grouped-query attention and other tricks to shrink the KV cache, and more recently state-space and hybrid architectures that make long context much cheaper.

And finally there's just economics and competition. There are a lot of providers now, open-weight models are strong, so margins get competed down.

When you multiply all of these, hardware maybe a few x, systems maybe 5 to 10x, models and architecture another 10x or more, you get these huge reductions. And I don't think we're done. Especially as workloads shift toward agents and reasoning, where you're generating tons of tokens, inference efficiency becomes the thing that matters most, so there's enormous incentive to keep pushing it down.

r002.rationale: It identifies decoding as memory-bound and points to memory bandwidth and KV-cache management as important inference concerns.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the headline number is that inference cost per token, for roughly the same level of capability, has dropped something like a hundredfold, maybe more, in the two or three years since ChatGPT came out. That's a crazy rate even by Moore's law standards, so it's worth breaking down where it actually came from. I'd say it's really three things stacking on top of each other.

The first is hardware. We went from A100s to H100s to Blackwell, and each generation gives you more FLOPs, more memory bandwidth, and lower precision formats, FP8 and now FP4. For inference specifically, a lot of the workload is memory-bandwidth bound, you're reading the weights and the KV cache over and over, so bandwidth improvements translate almost directly into cheaper tokens. That alone is maybe a 3 to 5x over this period.

The second is algorithms and systems, and that's the part I've spent most of my time on. Things like FlashAttention made the attention computation much more efficient and made long context practical. Then there's paged attention, continuous batching, speculative decoding, better quantization. And on the model architecture side, the shift to mixture of experts means you only activate a fraction of the parameters per token, so a frontier-quality model costs far less to serve. Multi-head latent attention, grouped query attention, these shrink the KV cache so you can batch way more requests on the same GPU. Each of these is a 1.5x or 2x, but they compound.

The third, which people underrate, is just that we got better at training. The models at a given capability level are smaller now. Better data, longer training, distillation from bigger models. So a model that matches the original ChatGPT is maybe 10 to 20x fewer active parameters. That's a direct cost reduction before you even touch the inference stack.

And then on top of all that there's competition. Once there are many providers serving comparable models, margins compress and prices track costs more closely. So some of the price decline is economics, not just engineering.

What I find interesting is that I don't think we're near the floor. The demand side is changing too, with reasoning models and agents generating way more tokens per task, so the pressure to drive cost down is only getting stronger. My guess is the next big gains come from hardware and algorithms being co-designed more tightly, rather than one side catching up to the other.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few things happening at once. One is that the hardware has gotten better. But a lot of the improvement comes from how efficiently we use that hardware. You can have a very powerful GPU and still spend a lot of time moving data around or waiting for memory instead of doing computation.

That’s where techniques like FlashAttention help: reorganizing the computation to reduce how much data you move. Then there are improvements at the serving level—batching requests together, managing the key-value cache more efficiently, and using lower precision. All of those let you serve more tokens on the same hardware.

The models are also getting better at a given size. For some tasks, a smaller model today can do what previously required a much larger model. That can make a big difference in cost.

And I’d distinguish the cost of running inference from the price you pay through an API. Competition influences that price too. So the decline is a combination of hardware, algorithms, systems engineering, and better models—not just one breakthrough.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a combination of several things. One is that the hardware has gotten better. But a lot of it is software: we’ve gotten much better at using the hardware we already have, through better kernels, better batching, and better ways to manage the KV cache.

For example, when you’re generating one token at a time, you often spend more time moving the model weights from memory than actually doing the computation. If you batch requests together, you can reuse those weights across more tokens. Quantization helps by reducing how much data you need to move. And techniques like FlashAttention reduce memory traffic for attention.

The models themselves have also become more efficient. You can get a given level of capability from a smaller model, which is a different source of savings from making the same model run faster.

So I wouldn’t attribute the decline to any single breakthrough. It’s improvements across the whole stack, plus competition pushing providers to pass those savings on. And the price per token isn’t quite the same as the cost of solving a task: if you use many more tokens for reasoning, your total bill can still go up.
